I'm 65 this year, and I've been working my 8 mu of land here in Quzhou County since I was a young man. My schooling stopped at middle school, but I know this soil and this climate better than any book ever could. The North China Plain gives us two crops a year if you don't waste time, and that's the system my family has followed for generations.

This year, I'm sticking with what I know works: winter wheat followed by summer maize. The wheat went into the ground last October, and it's greening up nicely now that spring is here. I'll nurse it through to harvest in early June, and the very next day I'll be getting the maize seed in the ground. In double-cropping, you can't afford to wait around. I thought about cotton like they grow down south, but at my age I don't have the back for all that picking, and the grain station always buys wheat and maize.

For the wheat, I buy improved seed from the agricultural supply shop. It's not the cheapest, but it performs well on my land. The extension fellow told me 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but I tried that three years ago and the yield was disappointing. Last year I put down about 20 kg per mu, split between base dressing and topdressing at green-up and jointing, and I got a much better crop. So I'm doing 20 kg N again, plus about 6 kg of phosphorus and 4 kg of potassium. The wheat will need three irrigations — green-up water, jointing, and heading — because the spring rain here is never enough. I'll spray twice for weeds and insects.

For the maize, I always use hybrid seed. The price hurts a little, but the yield advantage is too big to ignore. I'll apply about 18 kg of nitrogen, 5 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium. Two irrigations: one right after planting if the weather is dry, and one at the big trumpet stage. Two pesticide applications. Because the window between wheat harvest and maize planting is so tight — sometimes less than a week — I'm doing no-tillage planting for the maize. I can't risk missing the sowing window just to run the rotary tiller.

I'm expecting around 500 kg per mu from the wheat, and if the summer weather cooperates, about 550 kg per mu from the maize. That's not fancy, but it's honest work, and it's enough to keep this old farmer fed and with a little cash in pocket.
